# Who this is for

This is a short, code-level reference for anyone calling ZZedc's R
API directly against a study database -- for example to backfill a
field on a record that was created by a script rather than through
the Shiny application. If you operate the application as the
*content author* or *site coordinator* role instead, use the
*Request Correction* flow described in
[Content-Author Guide](content-author-guide.html), section 6.2, or
the "From the application" section below; both call the same
functions documented here from the application's UI.

# There is no direct update function

`data_entries` (see `ensure_data_entries_table()`,
`db_insert_data_entry()`) is insert-only: `entry_id` is its primary
key, and the package has no `db_update_data_entry()`. This is
deliberate, not an oversight. If code could silently overwrite a
submitted value, the audit trail (`audit_log`, written in the same
transaction as every insert) would no longer be a reliable record of
what was entered and when.

Editing a value that is already stored -- in `data_entries.data_json`
or in an ordinary column of any other table -- goes through the
**data-correction workflow** instead: `create_correction_request()`,
`approve_correction()`, `apply_correction()`. Each step is audited,
the three steps require two different user identities (the requester
cannot approve their own request), and the change is only written to
the table once it has been approved.

# One-time setup

The correction tables (`correction_requests`, `correction_history`,
`correction_approvers`, `correction_overrides`) are provisioned the
same way `data_entries` is: idempotently, from a raw connection.

```{r}
library(zzedc)

init_data_correction(db_path = "data/study.db")
```

If your script never opened a connection through `get_db_adapter()`
first (for example a bare `DBI::dbConnect()` against a SQLite file
outside the Shiny app), warm the adapter cache before calling any
`zzedc` database function, or you will see
`"Configuration file must have a 'database' section"`:

```{r}
invisible(get_db_adapter(
  config = list(db_backend = "sqlite", sqlite = list(path = "data/study.db")),
  force_new = TRUE
))
```

# The three-step workflow

## 1. Request the correction

`create_correction_request()` takes the table, the record's primary
key, the field name, the value currently stored, and the value it
should become. `correction_reason` must be one of the codes from
`get_correction_reasons()` (`TYPO`, `SOURCE_DOC_ERROR`,
`CALCULATION_ERROR`, `TRANSCRIPTION_ERROR`, `UNIT_ERROR`,
`DATE_ERROR`, `PROTOCOL_CLARIFICATION`, `QUERY_RESPONSE`, or `OTHER`
with `reason_details` of at least 10 characters).

For a field stored inside `data_entries.data_json` (rather than a
real column), `record_id` is the entry's `entry_id` and `field_name`
is the JSON key -- the function resolves which case it is
automatically.

```{r}
req <- create_correction_request(
  table_name        = "data_entries",
  record_id         = "DE-20261116232516273-8841",
  field_name        = "manuscript_id",
  original_value    = "",
  corrected_value   = "ALZRT-D-26-00142",
  correction_reason = "SOURCE_DOC_ERROR",
  reason_details    = "Manuscript ID was unknown when the review was logged; now confirmed from the editor's acknowledgment e-mail.",
  requested_by      = "rgt"
)
req$request_id
```

`original_value` is what the field holds *right now*. If the field
is currently blank or was never set, pass `""` or leave it `NA` --
`apply_correction()` treats a missing stored value as matching a
missing or empty `original_value`.

## 2. Approve it

A different user than `requested_by` must approve:

```{r}
approve_correction(
  request_id      = req$request_id,
  reviewed_by     = "study_manager",
  review_comments = "Confirmed against the acknowledgment e-mail."
)
```

Passing `reviewer_role` additionally checks that the reviewer holds
one of `"Admin"`, `"PI"`, `"StudyManager"`, or `"Data Manager"`.
`reject_correction()` is the alternative when the change should not
go through; it requires a comment of at least 10 characters.

## 3. Apply it

```{r}
result <- apply_correction(
  request_id   = req$request_id,
  applied_by   = "study_manager",
  applier_role = "Study Manager"
)
result$status        # "APPLIED"
result$old_value      # ""
result$new_value      # "ALZRT-D-26-00142"
```

`apply_correction()` re-reads the record inside the same transaction
as the write and refuses to apply if the field's current value no
longer matches `original_value` -- someone else changed it since the
request was opened. On success it writes the `UPDATE` audit record
and, when `record_versions` is available, stores a before/after
version pair.

`applier_role` is optional (default `NULL`, which skips the check --
every call above that omits it keeps working exactly as before this
parameter existed) but, when given, is checked against the same
allowed set `approve_correction()`'s `reviewer_role` already uses
(`"Admin"`, `"PI"`, `"StudyManager"`, `"Data Manager"`). Before
2026-11-17, approval was role-gated but applying an already-approved
correction was not -- any authenticated caller could write the new
value regardless of role. A script that calls `apply_correction()`
directly should pass `applier_role` for the same reason a person
using the application's Corrections tab now only sees an *Apply
Correction* control when their own role is one of the four above.

# From the application

The application's Corrections tab (`data_correction_ui()`/
`data_correction_server()`, mounted under the Admin dropdown) wraps
the same three functions in a UI, with two entry points:

- From the EDC tab, a form's entries table (right below where you
  enter data for that form) has a *Request Correction* button on
  each row. Clicking it switches to the Corrections tab with that
  record already selected -- the entry point this vignette's
  `record_id` example above stands in for when called from a
  script instead.
- From the Corrections tab directly, under *Create Request*: set
  Table Name to `data_entries` and Record ID to the entry's
  identifier, and the Field and Corrected Value controls become a
  dropdown of that record's own fields and a typed input matching
  the selected field's type (a RADIO field gets radio buttons, a
  DATE field gets a date picker, and so on) -- the same validation
  `validate_crf_submission()` performs here is exactly the
  structural check this vignette's R-level calls skip past, so a
  value the original form would have rejected is rejected here too,
  before a request is even created. Any table other than
  `data_entries` falls back to plain text fields, matching the
  R-level calls above exactly.

Approve, reject, and apply all happen from the same tab's *Pending
Review* view, and an *Apply Correction* control only appears for a
logged-in role in the allowed set described above.

# Locked records

A record locked via the *Lock Visit* control (see
[Content-Author Guide](content-author-guide.html), section 6.3), or
one held by another user's `version_locks` entry, cannot be corrected
through steps 1-3 alone. `apply_correction()` returns
`requires_override = TRUE`; an administrator must first call
`request_correction_override()` and `approve_override()` for that
specific request before `apply_correction()` is retried.

# What the workflow will not let you touch

`apply_correction()` refuses to act on `audit_log`, `audit_chain`,
`audit_events`, `record_versions`, `version_locks`, `edc_users`,
`electronic_signatures`, or `data_entries_audit` -- and on a table's
primary-key column or on `data_json` as a whole (only a named field
*inside* `data_json` can be corrected, never the blob itself). These
are the records the audit trail depends on; correcting them through
this path would undermine the thing the path exists to guarantee.
